newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts confident about ABB despite 1996 result.
newsitem.headline: Analysts confident about ABB despite 1996 result.

text.p: Industry analysts remain confident about the earnings prospects of ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG despite a somewhat disappointing 1996 result.
Emerging from a briefing by ABB executives, analysts said the stock market's negative reaction to ABB's result and 1997 forecast was excessive, but understandable in light of the high expectations.
"The market had forgotten how intense competition is," said Frederick Hasslauer of Bank Sal. Oppenheim, adding that other companies could also dash expectations.
"The market has become overheated," said Peter Gachnang of Bank Julius Baer.
But instead of blaming ABB for their expectations, analysts said they had been too optimistic and ABB had often warned that 1996 and 1997 would be tough years.
"Expectations were too optimistic," said Otto Lehmann of Rotschild Bank AG, adding the results were below these expectations and that triggered a drop in share prices.
"We can't blame the company," said Thomas Pfyl of Bank Vontobel, noting ABB's warnings about the effect Europe's sluggish economy would have on ABB.
"Expectations were slightly frothy" said Russ Mould of SBC Warburg, adding that ABBs' shares are likely to perform in line with the market over the next six months.
"The stock will reflect that this is one of the quieter years," said Mould.
Analysts said they would adjust their earnings forecast downward slightly for 1997 and 1998 and this would likely put the shares of ABB's two quoted parent companies under some short-term pressure.
But while forecasts will be cut slightly, analysts are unlikely to change their recommendations of the stock. Most analysts have ABB on a buy recommendation.
"Following ABB's presentation, I am less negative than just after the figures," said Paola Orler of Zurich Kantonalbank.
After some pressure the shares of Sweden's ABB AB and Switzerland's ABB AG were likely to rebound later as the market digests the better prospects for 1998 and onwards, analysts added.

Earlier today ABB reported a 6.2 percent decline in 1996 net profit to $1.23 billion. However, when the 1996 result is compared with the adjusted 1995 profit number, the profit actually rose 15.8 percent.
The 1995 profit was inflated by a one-time gain of $250 million from the Adtranz transportation venture with Germany's Daimler-Benz AG.
On average analysts had forecast a 1996 net profit of $1.30 billion.
The stock market's disappointment with ABB came immediately and on the Swiss Exchange the shares of the Swiss parent company ended 5.3 percent lower at 1,714 francs.
